title: Message Queues, Streams & Event-Driven Patterns
summary: Complete guide to async communication — Kafka internals (partitions, offsets, ISR, leader election, KRaft), RabbitMQ exchanges, SQS, event-driven patterns (Event Sourcing, CQRS, Outbox, Saga), and when to use each.

explanation.overview: In a monolithic application, components call each other directly via function calls. In a distributed system with microservices, direct synchronous calls create tight coupling, cascading failures, and throughput bottlenecks. Message queues and event streams decouple producers from consumers, enable asynchronous processing, and absorb traffic spikes. This is one of the most important topics in system design — nearly every large-scale system uses some form of async messaging.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: At its core, a message queue is a FIFO buffer: producers write messages, consumers read them. The queue persists messages until they're consumed. The key difference between a 'message queue' (RabbitMQ, SQS) and a 'streaming platform' (Kafka) is that queues deliver each message to ONE consumer (point-to-point) and remove it after consumption, while streams retain messages in an ordered log and allow multiple consumer groups to independently read at their own pace.

children.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication
children.summary: Why async communication matters and when to use sync (HTTP/gRPC) vs async (queue/stream).

explanation.overview: Synchronous (request-response): Service A calls Service B and WAITS for a response before continuing. Example: user clicks 'Place Order' → Order Service synchronously calls Payment Service → waits for payment result → returns to user. Pros: simple, immediate feedback. Cons: if Payment Service is slow (2 seconds) or down, the user waits or gets an error. Caller and callee are tightly coupled — both must be available simultaneously. Asynchronous (fire-and-forget or event-driven): Service A publishes a message/event and continues immediately without waiting. Example: user clicks 'Place Order' → Order Service writes order to DB, publishes 'OrderCreated' event to Kafka → returns 'Order received' to user immediately → Payment Service consumes the event and processes payment in the background → notifies user via email/push when payment completes.

key_concepts.definition: Use synchronous calls when: (1) The caller NEEDS the result immediately to continue (validating a credit card number, fetching user profile to display). (2) The operation is fast (< 100ms). (3) Failure must be communicated to the user immediately. (4) The two services are in the same trust boundary and low latency path.

Use asynchronous messaging when: (1) The operation is slow (video transcoding, email sending, PDF generation). (2) The caller doesn't need the result immediately (order confirmation email). (3) You need to absorb traffic spikes (100K orders/minute during flash sale → queue absorbs, workers process at steady rate). (4) You need to decouple services (Order Service shouldn't break if Email Service is down). (5) You need fan-out (one event consumed by multiple services: analytics, notification, billing).

When the consumer can't keep up with the producer. In sync: the caller gets timeouts or 503s. In async: the queue grows. Back pressure strategies: (1) Queue size limit with rejection (producer gets 'queue full' error). (2) Rate limiting producers. (3) Auto-scaling consumers. (4) Dropping low-priority messages. Kafka handles back pressure naturally — consumers pull at their own pace, and Kafka retains messages based on retention policy (7 days by default).

children.title: Apache Kafka — Deep Dive Internals
children.summary: How Kafka achieves millions of messages/sec — its internal log structure, partition-based parallelism, replication with ISR, and the new KRaft consensus mode.

explanation.overview: Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform designed for high-throughput, fault-tolerant, real-time data pipelines. Unlike traditional message queues that delete messages after consumption, Kafka retains messages in an ordered, immutable, append-only log. Consumers track their position (offset) and can re-read historical data. This log-based design is what makes Kafka fundamentally different and powerful.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: A Kafka cluster consists of multiple brokers (servers). Data is organized into topics. Each topic is divided into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, immutable sequence of records, physically stored as a segment of log files on disk. Producers choose which partition to write to. Consumers read from partitions using offsets.

children.title: Topics, Partitions & Offsets
children.summary: How Kafka organizes data into topics and partitions, and how offsets track consumer position.

explanation.overview: A Topic is a logical category (like 'orders', 'user-events', 'page-views'). Each topic is split into one or more Partitions — each partition is an independent ordered log stored on a single broker. Partitions enable parallelism: with 12 partitions, up to 12 consumers can read in parallel.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: PRODUCING: When a producer sends a message, it must choose a partition. Three strategies: (1) Round-robin — distribute messages across partitions evenly (best throughput). (2) Key-based — hash(message_key) % num_partitions. All messages with the same key go to the same partition, guaranteeing ordering for that key. Example: hash(user_id) ensures all events for user 123 go to partition 7 in order. (3) Custom partitioner — application logic decides. OFFSET: Each message within a partition gets a monotonically increasing offset (0, 1, 2, ...). This is the message's unique ID within its partition. Consumers track their 'current offset' — the last message they've processed. Offsets are stored in a special internal topic: __consumer_offsets (log-compacted). CONSUMING: Consumers pull messages from Kafka (not pushed). A consumer group assigns each partition to exactly one consumer in the group. With 12 partitions and 3 consumers: each consumer reads 4 partitions. If a consumer dies, its partitions are rebalanced to surviving consumers. You can NEVER have more consumers than partitions in a group — extra consumers sit idle. ORDERING GUARANTEE: Messages within a single partition are strictly ordered. NO ordering guarantee across partitions. So if you need global ordering, use 1 partition (sacrifices parallelism) or key-based partitioning for per-key ordering.

key_concepts.definition: Start with: partitions = max(expected_throughput_MB_per_sec / 10, expected_consumer_count). Each partition can handle ~10 MB/s writes. Too few partitions = throughput bottleneck. Too many = more file handles, longer leader elections, more memory on brokers. Industry practice: start with 6-12 partitions, increase later if needed. WARNING: increasing partitions is easy; decreasing is impossible without recreating the topic.

When consumers join/leave a group, Kafka reassigns partitions. During rebalancing (which takes seconds to minutes), consumption pauses. Strategies: (1) Eager rebalancing (default in older versions) — revoke all partitions, reassign all. Causes full stop-the-world. (2) Cooperative rebalancing (incremental, Kafka 2.4+) — only revoke affected partitions. Much shorter disruption. CONFIGURABLE: session.timeout.ms = time before Kafka considers a consumer dead (default 45s). heartbeat.interval.ms = how often consumer sends heartbeat (default 3s, must be < session.timeout/3).

configurable_params.name: num.partitions
configurable_params.effect: More partitions = more parallelism but more overhead.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Rule: partitions ≥ consumer instances. Start with 6-12. Can't decrease later.

configurable_params.name: retention.ms
configurable_params.effect: How long messages are retained. After this, they're eligible for deletion.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Longer retention = more disk. Shorter = risk of data loss if consumers fall behind.

configurable_params.name: max.message.bytes
configurable_params.effect: Maximum size of a single message.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Large messages reduce throughput and increase latency. For large payloads, use claim check pattern — store data in S3 and pass the S3 URL in the message.

children.title: Replication, ISR & Leader Election
children.summary: How Kafka replicates data for durability and performs leader election when brokers fail.

explanation.overview: Each partition has multiple replicas distributed across different brokers. One replica is the Leader (handles all reads and writes), and the rest are Followers (passively replicate the leader's log). This provides fault tolerance — if the leader broker crashes, a follower is promoted to leader.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: REPLICATION FLOW: (1) Producer sends message to the partition's Leader broker. (2) Leader appends message to its local log. (3) Followers pull the message from the leader and append to their logs. (4) When all ISR (In-Sync Replicas) have acknowledged, the message is 'committed'. (5) Only committed messages are visible to consumers. ISR (IN-SYNC REPLICAS): The set of replicas that are 'caught up' with the leader — their log end offset is within replica.lag.time.max.ms (default 30s) of the leader's. If a follower falls behind (slow network, disk issue), it's removed from ISR. When it catches up, it's added back. KEY SETTING: min.insync.replicas (default 1). If set to 2, the producer must receive acknowledgment from at least 2 ISR members before the write is considered successful. With acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2 and replication.factor=3: the write succeeds as long as 2 out of 3 replicas are in sync. If only 1 is in sync, the write fails (NotEnoughReplicasException) — preventing data loss at the cost of availability. LEADER ELECTION: A special broker called the Controller monitors all broker health via heartbeats. When a leader broker fails: (1) Controller detects the failure. (2) Controller selects a new leader from the ISR list (the replica with the most recent data). (3) Controller updates the cluster metadata and notifies all brokers. (4) Clients (producers and consumers) query metadata and redirect to the new leader. Leadership transfer takes 5-30 seconds depending on controller responsiveness and number of affected partitions. UNCLEAN LEADER ELECTION (unclean.leader.election.enable, default false): if ALL ISR replicas are down and only out-of-sync replicas remain, should Kafka elect one? If yes (true): data loss (messages acknowledged to ISR but not replicated to the now-elected leader are lost). If no (false): the partition stays offline until an ISR replica comes back. Choose based on your durability requirements — financial systems = false. Log analytics = true.

key_concepts.definition: Historically, Kafka used Apache ZooKeeper for controller election, broker registration, and cluster metadata. Problems: ZooKeeper is a separate system to manage, limits scaling (ZooKeeper bottlenecks with millions of partitions), and adds operational complexity. KRaft (Kafka Raft) replaces ZooKeeper entirely. A quorum of controller nodes (typically 3) manages cluster metadata using the Raft consensus protocol. Metadata is stored in a Kafka internal topic (__cluster_metadata). Benefits: simplified operations (no more ZooKeeper), faster controller failover (seconds vs minutes), support for millions of partitions. As of Kafka 3.6+, KRaft is production-ready and ZooKeeper is deprecated.

acks=0: producer doesn't wait for any acknowledgment. Fire-and-forget. Fastest but messages can be lost. Use for: metrics/logs where loss is acceptable. acks=1: producer waits for leader acknowledgment only. If leader crashes after ack but before replication, message is lost. Use for: most general workloads (balanced speed and durability). acks=all (or -1): producer waits for ALL ISR replicas to acknowledge. Slowest but strongest durability. Combined with min.insync.replicas=2, provides strong durability guarantee. Use for: financial transactions, critical events.

configurable_params.name: replication.factor
configurable_params.effect: Number of copies of each partition. Industry standard: 3.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Higher = more durability + more disk usage + higher write latency. 3 is the universal standard — can survive 1 broker failure with no data loss.

configurable_params.name: min.insync.replicas
configurable_params.effect: Minimum ISR count for acks=all writes to succeed.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Set to 2 with replication.factor=3 for strong durability. Setting equal to replication.factor means writes fail if ANY replica is down.

configurable_params.name: replica.lag.time.max.ms
configurable_params.effect: If a follower hasn't fetched from leader within this time, it's removed from ISR.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Lower = faster detection of slow replicas but more ISR churn. Higher = more tolerant of temporary network blips.

children.title: Delivery Semantics — At-Most-Once, At-Least-Once, Exactly-Once
children.summary: The three delivery guarantees in messaging systems and how Kafka achieves exactly-once processing.

explanation.overview: Every messaging system must choose among three delivery semantics. The choice fundamentally affects your system's correctness.

key_concepts.definition: A message is delivered zero or one times. It may be lost but never duplicated. Implementation: producer sends message with acks=0 (fire-and-forget) or consumer commits offset BEFORE processing. If consumer crashes after commit but before processing, the message is skipped on restart. Use for: metrics, logs, analytics where losing a few data points is acceptable.

A message is delivered one or more times. It's never lost but may be duplicated. Implementation: producer retries on failure (retries=MAX_INT, acks=all). Consumer processes message FIRST, then commits offset. If consumer crashes after processing but before commit, the message is re-processed on restart. This is the DEFAULT behavior in most Kafka setups. The consumer must be idempotent — processing the same message twice should produce the same result. Example idempotent operation: SET user_balance = 100 (always results in 100). NOT idempotent: INCREMENT user_balance BY 50 (double-processing adds 100).

A message is delivered and processed exactly once. No loss, no duplication. This is the hardest guarantee and most systems don't need it. How Kafka achieves it: (1) Idempotent Producer (enable.idempotence=true): Kafka assigns each producer a PID (producer ID) and each message a sequence number. If a retry sends the same message again, the broker detects the duplicate via PID+sequence and silently drops it. This gives exactly-once WITHIN a single partition. (2) Kafka Transactions (transactional.id=my-app): wraps produce + consumer offset commit into an atomic transaction. Either ALL messages are produced AND offsets committed, or NONE are. The consumer reads with isolation.level=read_committed to only see committed transactional messages. Use for: stream processing (read from topic A → process → write to topic B) where duplicates are unacceptable. TRADE-OFF: transactions add latency (~50-100ms per batch) and reduce throughput by ~20-30%. Most applications don't need exactly-once — at-least-once with idempotent consumers is simpler and sufficient.

advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: When you need at-least-once delivery but your processing isn't naturally idempotent
advanced_tweaks.how: Store a deduplication table (message_id → processed_at) in your database. Before processing, check if message_id exists. If yes, skip. If no, process and insert. Use a unique message ID from the producer (UUID or partition+offset). Wrap the check + process + insert in a database transaction. This gives you exactly-once processing semantics without Kafka transactions.

advanced_tweaks.technique: Outbox Pattern for reliable event publishing
advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: When a service must write to DB AND publish an event, and both must succeed or both fail
advanced_tweaks.how: Instead of writing to DB and then publishing to Kafka (which can fail between the two), write to DB AND insert into an 'outbox' table in the SAME database transaction. A separate relay process (or CDC via Debezium) reads the outbox table and publishes to Kafka. If publishing fails, it retries from the outbox. This guarantees: if DB write succeeds, the event will eventually be published.

children.title: RabbitMQ vs Kafka vs SQS — When to Use Each
children.summary: Detailed comparison of the three most common messaging systems with concrete guidance on when to use each.

explanation.overview: These three systems are often confused but serve different use cases. The key differences are in message retention, delivery model, ordering guarantees, and operational complexity.

key_concepts.definition: Traditional message broker implementing AMQP protocol. ARCHITECTURE: Producers → Exchange → Queue → Consumer. Exchanges route messages to queues based on rules. Exchange types: Direct (exact routing key match), Fanout (broadcast to all bound queues), Topic (pattern-based routing like 'order.*.created'), Headers (match on message headers). DELIVERY MODEL: Push-based — broker pushes messages to consumers. Smart broker, dumb consumer. Message acknowledged then deleted. No replay capability. ORDERING: Guaranteed within a single queue (FIFO). Not guaranteed across queues. THROUGHPUT: ~20K-50K messages/sec per node (depends on persistence and message size). Much lower than Kafka. PERSISTENCE: messages can be durable (written to disk) or transient (memory only). STRENGTHS: Complex routing rules (topic exchange with wildcards), per-message acknowledgment, priority queues, TTL per message, delayed message delivery. USE WHEN: task queues (background jobs with different priorities), complex routing logic ('route all European orders to EU payment processor queue'), RPC-style request/reply patterns.

Distributed event streaming platform. ARCHITECTURE: Producers → Topic (partitioned log) → Consumer Groups. No routing logic — producers choose a partition, consumers read from assigned partitions. DELIVERY MODEL: Pull-based — consumers pull messages at their own pace. Dumb broker, smart consumer. Messages are retained for a configurable period (default 7 days) regardless of consumption. Multiple consumer groups can read the same topic independently — each at their own offset. ORDERING: Guaranteed within a partition. Per-key ordering with key-based partitioning. THROUGHPUT: ~100K-1M+ messages/sec per broker. Orders of magnitude higher than RabbitMQ. Optimized for sequential disk I/O (append-only writes, OS page cache). REPLAY: consumers can seek to any offset and re-process historical data. This is impossible with RabbitMQ/SQS. STRENGTHS: massive throughput, event replay, log compaction (keep latest value per key), stream processing (Kafka Streams, ksqlDB), exactly-once transactions. USE WHEN: high-throughput event streaming (clickstream, logs, IoT telemetry), event sourcing, real-time data pipelines, any scenario where you need to replay events or have multiple independent consumers.

Fully managed message queue by AWS. Two types: Standard (best-effort ordering, at-least-once delivery, nearly unlimited throughput) and FIFO (strict ordering by message group ID, exactly-once, 3000 messages/sec with batching). DELIVERY MODEL: Pull-based. Message becomes 'invisible' when a consumer receives it (visibility timeout, default 30 seconds). If not deleted within timeout, it reappears for another consumer. After a configurable number of receives (maxReceiveCount), message goes to Dead Letter Queue (DLQ). NO message replay — deleted after successful consumption. STRENGTHS: zero operations (fully managed by AWS), auto-scaling (never worry about provisioning), DLQ built-in, integrates with Lambda (event-driven processing), extremely reliable. USE WHEN: simple async task processing in AWS (send email on order, process image upload), you want zero operational overhead, workloads that don't need replay or complex routing. LIMITATIONS: max message size 256 KB (use S3 for larger payloads with claim check pattern), no routing logic (one queue = one consumer type).

pros: Kafka: highest throughput, replay, multiple consumers
RabbitMQ: flexible routing, priority queues, mature ecosystem
SQS: zero ops, infinite scale, DLQ built-in
cons: Kafka: complex operations, steep learning curve, overkill for simple tasks
RabbitMQ: lower throughput, no replay, operational burden
SQS: AWS lock-in, no replay, limited ordering (FIFO capped at 3K/sec)
tradeoffs.when_to_use: Kafka for high-throughput event streaming and replay. RabbitMQ for complex routing and task queues. SQS for simple AWS-native async processing.
tradeoffs.when_to_avoid: Kafka for simple job queues (<1K/sec). RabbitMQ for >100K messages/sec. SQS when you need message replay or non-AWS deployment.

children.title: Event-Driven Architecture Patterns
children.summary: Advanced patterns for building event-driven systems — Event Sourcing, CQRS, Transactional Outbox, and Saga for distributed transactions.

explanation.overview: These patterns appear in almost every Staff/Principal-level system design interview. They solve the fundamental challenges of data consistency, service decoupling, and audit trails in distributed systems.

children.title: Event Sourcing
children.summary: Instead of storing current state, store the complete history of state changes as an immutable sequence of events.

explanation.overview: Traditional: store the current state (account_balance = $500). Event Sourcing: store every event that led to the current state (deposited $1000, withdrew $300, deposited $200, withdrew $400 → balance = $500). The current state is derived by replaying all events.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: Events are immutable facts stored in an append-only log (event store). Each event has: event_id, aggregate_id (the entity it belongs to, e.g., account_123), event_type (AccountCredited, AccountDebited), timestamp, and payload (amount, description). To get the current state: load all events for aggregate_id, replay them in order, accumulate state. This is called 'rehydration'. For performance, periodically save snapshots (current state at event offset N). To rehydrate: load latest snapshot + replay events after snapshot offset. WHY: (1) Complete audit trail — you know exactly what happened and when (regulatory compliance, financial systems). (2) Time travel — reconstruct state at any point in time. (3) Debug by replaying events. (4) No destructive updates — events are never modified or deleted. (5) Easy to add new read models by replaying events through a new projection. TRADEOFF: Complexity — querying the current state is harder (must replay or use projections). Schema evolution is tricky (events are immutable; old events follow old schemas). Eventual consistency between event store and projections.

examples.title: Banking Example
examples.description: Events: [{type: 'AccountOpened', balance: 0}, {type: 'Deposited', amount: 1000}, {type: 'Withdrew', amount: 200}, {type: 'Deposited', amount: 500}]. Current balance = 0 + 1000 - 200 + 500 = $1300. If auditor asks 'what happened on March 5?', filter events by timestamp.

use_cases.why: Regulatory requirement to maintain complete transaction history. Event sourcing provides a natural audit log.
Track every add/remove/quantity change. Can analyze abandonment patterns by replaying cart events.
Git IS event sourcing — each commit is an immutable event. The working directory is derived by replaying commits.

children.title: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
children.summary: Separate the write path (commands) from the read path (queries), allowing each to be independently optimized and scaled.

explanation.overview: In a traditional CRUD system, the same database model handles both writes and reads. This creates conflicts: writes want normalized data (3NF) for consistency; reads want denormalized data for fast queries. CQRS separates them: the WRITE side (Command Model) handles mutations through commands (CreateOrder, UpdateInventory) and stores data in a write-optimized format (normalized relational DB, event store). The READ side (Query Model) handles queries and stores data in precomputed, denormalized read models optimized for specific query patterns (Elasticsearch for search, Redis for feeds, materialized views for dashboards).
explanation.how_it_works_internally: WRITE flow: Client → Command Handler → validate business rules → persist to write DB → publish event (OrderCreated). READ flow: Event Consumer → update read model(s) → Client queries read model directly. The read models are eventually consistent with the write model (delay of milliseconds to seconds). Multiple read models can exist for different query patterns: read model 1 in Elasticsearch for full-text search, read model 2 in Redis sorted set for leaderboards, read model 3 in Postgres materialized view for analytics dashboards. WHEN TO USE: (1) Read patterns differ significantly from write patterns. (2) Read and write loads are asymmetric (10:1 or higher). (3) You need different storage technologies for different query types. (4) Often combined with Event Sourcing — events from the event store are projected into read models. WHEN NOT TO USE: simple CRUD with similar read/write patterns and modest scale. CQRS adds complexity (two models to maintain, eventual consistency to handle).

use_cases.why: Write model: normalized relational DB for product CRUD. Read model 1: Elasticsearch for search with filters. Read model 2: Redis for 'frequently bought together' recommendations. Read model 3: denormalized JSON in CDN for product detail pages.
Write model: Postgres for posts (user_id, content, timestamp). Read model: Redis sorted set per user containing their precomputed feed — tweets from people they follow, sorted by time.

children.title: Saga Pattern — Distributed Transactions Without 2PC
children.summary: A sequence of local transactions across services, where each step has a compensating action for rollback.

explanation.overview: In a microservice architecture, a single business operation (placing an order) may span multiple services (Order Service, Inventory Service, Payment Service, Shipping Service). You can't use a database transaction across service boundaries. 2PC (Two-Phase Commit) is an option but it's slow, blocking, and the coordinator is a single point of failure. The Saga pattern breaks the operation into a sequence of local transactions. If any step fails, previously completed steps are undone via compensating transactions.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: EXAMPLE — Place Order Saga: Step 1: Order Service creates order (status: PENDING). Step 2: Inventory Service reserves items. Step 3: Payment Service charges credit card. Step 4: Order Service confirms order (status: CONFIRMED). Step 5: Shipping Service schedules delivery. If Step 3 (payment) fails: Compensate Step 2: Inventory Service releases reserved items. Compensate Step 1: Order Service marks order as FAILED. TWO STYLES: (1) Choreography: each service publishes events and other services react. Order Service publishes OrderCreated → Inventory Service subscribes, reserves items, publishes ItemsReserved → Payment Service subscribes, charges card, publishes PaymentCompleted → Order Service subscribes, confirms order. No central coordinator. Each service knows its own business logic. PROS: loosely coupled. CONS: hard to trace the flow, hard to debug, circular dependencies can emerge. (2) Orchestration: a central Saga Orchestrator sends commands to each service and handles responses. Orchestrator → 'Reserve items' → Inventory Service → 'Items reserved' → Orchestrator → 'Charge card' → Payment Service → 'Payment failed' → Orchestrator → 'Release items' → Inventory Service. PROS: clear flow, easy to debug, centralized error handling. CONS: orchestrator is a SPOF, tight coupling to orchestrator. INDUSTRY STANDARD: Use orchestration for complex sagas (>3 steps) and choreography for simple ones (2-3 steps). Temporal.io and AWS Step Functions are popular orchestration frameworks.

use_cases.why: Spans order, inventory, payment, shipping services. Each has its own DB. Saga ensures all steps complete or all are rolled back.
Book flight + hotel + car rental across different provider APIs. If hotel booking fails, cancel the flight booking (compensating transaction).
